title: ר' יהושוע בן לוי
author: Heilprin source tradition; Warsaw digital witness

paragraphs: (1) He was one of the amoraim: so writes Rashi in the chapter Kol HaYad, 18b, beginning. But Maimonides counted him among the tannaim. Megalleh Amukkot, manner 223, cites Halikhot Olam in Maimonides’ name that Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi all belonged to the first generation of amoraim. He appears at the end of the Mishnah and in the chapter Shanu Chakhamim, which is composed of baraitot. Yuchasin, in the sequence of tannaim, introduction to the letter yod, writes: at the end of Uktzin, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that the Holy One, blessed be He, will bequeath 310 worlds to each righteous person. Although he was an amora, they included him there; perhaps he said this before Rabbi, and they wrote it in his name, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was older than Rabbi Yochanan, and Rabbi Yochanan read before Rabbi. End quotation. See above, under Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, what I wrote in Tosafot’s name: in several instances the sages incorporated amoraim’s statements in the Mishnah. See also Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi.

(2) He was a Levite, as related in the chapter HaZeroa. [It is not there, but in the chapter Kol HaBasar, 106b:] Meyasha, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s grandson, was a Levite; see his entry. Megalleh Amukkot 223 explains ‘You have begun to show Your servant’ precisely, in accordance with ‘the Levite shall serve’: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was among the gatekeepers; see there. This is very puzzling, for he lived long after the destruction, whereas Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah was a singer in the Temple. In the Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Ein Omdin, mishnah 5, and Gittin, the chapter HaNizakin, halakhah 9, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: ‘I never recited the blessing before a priest, nor did an Israelite recite it before me.’ Beer Sheva, Horayot, chapter 3, writes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was a Levite. See Tur, Orach Chayim, end of section 11, in the name of Maharam of Rothenburg; so too the Rosh, Gittin, end of HaNizakin. Beit Yosef, Orach Chayim, section 135, quotes the Rosh as saying that Megillah 28 has Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s ‘I never recited the blessing,’ and so forth. It is not found in Megillah, but in the Jerusalem Talmud cited above. See Jerusalem Talmud, Maaser Sheni 5:5: in his days they wished to take a vote not to give the tithe to the priesthood. They said: ‘Who will go in? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi supports the Levites.’ Gilgulei Neshamot (cited as ג״נ) writes: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is Kehat, for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was not a Levite but an Israelite. They wished to teach that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was literally a son of Levi, in that he was Kehat.’ End quotation. This contradicts what was said above.

(3) He entered the Garden of Eden during his lifetime. In Chelek, 98a, he found Elijah standing at the gates of the Garden of Eden. He asked: ‘When will the Messiah come?’ He replied: ‘When this Master desires it’—the Divine Presence was with them. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: ‘I saw two and heard the voice of a third,’ for the Divine Presence was beside them. Again he found Elijah standing at the entrance to Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s cave. He asked: ‘Shall I come to the world to come?’ He replied: ‘If this Master desires it.’ ‘I saw two,’ and so forth. He asked: ‘When will the Messiah come?’ He replied: ‘Go ask him himself’—the Messiah. ‘Where does he sit?’ In the Garden of Eden, on the side opposite Rome’s gates, and so forth. He went to him and said: ‘Peace upon you, my master and teacher.’ He replied: ‘Peace upon you, son of Levi.’ He asked: ‘When will the master come?’ He replied: ‘Today.’ He returned to Elijah, who asked: ‘What did he tell you?’ He replied: ‘Peace upon you, son of Levi.’ He said: ‘He has assured you and your father of the world to come: were you not completely righteous, he would not have greeted you or mentioned your father’s name.’ He said: ‘He has deceived me, for he said he would come today and did not come.’ He replied: ‘This is what he told you: “Today, if you listen to His voice.”’ In the chapter HaMaddir, 77b: ‘Beware of the flies of those afflicted with raatan’—the flies settle upon them and bring the disease to another person. Rabbi Zeira would not sit in its wind; Rabbi Elazar would not enter his tent; Rav Ammi and Rav Assi would not eat eggs from that alley. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would attach himself to them, staying close to them, and engage in Torah, for Torah protects. When he was dying—when his time to depart arrived—they told the Angel of Death: ‘Go do his will.’ He went and appeared to him. He said: ‘Show me my place’—take me to the Garden of Eden and show me my place. He replied, ‘Very well.’ ‘Give me your knife, lest you frighten me on the road.’ He gave it to him. When they reached there, he lifted him to show him. He leapt and fell to the other side. He seized him by the corner of his cloak. He said: ‘I swear that I shall not come back.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said: ‘If he has ever sought release from an oath, let him return; otherwise, let him not return.’ He said: ‘Give me my knife.’ He would not give it to him. A heavenly voice went forth: ‘Return it to him, for it is needed for the creatures.’ Elijah proclaimed before him: ‘Make room for the son of Levi! Make room,’ and so forth. He went and found Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai sitting upon thirteen golden thrones. He asked: ‘Are you the son of Levi?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ ‘Was a rainbow seen in your days?’ He replied, ‘Yes.’ ‘If so, you are not the son of Levi.’ But that was not so: no rainbow had appeared; he merely thought, ‘I shall not claim merit for myself.’ In Kol Bo and Shibbolei HaLeket, with part also cited in Shalshelet HaKabbalah 91a, in the name of Tractate Garden of Eden: when his time to depart the world arrived, the Holy One, blessed be He, told the Angel of Death: ‘Do for him whatever he asks of you,’ and so forth. The Angel of Death came and said: ‘Your time has arrived,’ and so forth, ‘but anything you ask of me I shall do.’ He replied: ‘I ask you to show me my place in the Garden of Eden,’ and so forth. Elijah proclaimed before him, telling the righteous: ‘Make room,’ and so forth. He found Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, and so forth. The Angel of Death went to Rabban Gamliel and said: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi has done this to me.’ Rabban Gamliel told him: ‘He did well. But come, I shall send you to him.’ He told him: ‘Please search the Garden of Eden, Gehinnom, and their storehouses; write it down and send it to me: are there gentiles in the Garden of Eden, and Israelites in Gehinnom?’ The Angel of Death went and told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. He said: ‘I shall do so.’ Rabbi Yehoshua went and searched the Garden of Eden and found seven houses there; each house was 120,000 mil in length and breadth, and so forth. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: ‘I wished to measure Gehinnom and see it, but they did not give me permission, because the righteous shall not see Gehinnom. I sent that angel, whose name was Komam, to write down all of Gehinnom for me, but he could not: at that moment they killed Rabbi Yishmael the high priest, Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel, and ten righteous men. The report arrived, and I could not go with that angel to Gehinnom. One day I stood and received with the angel Kinnor [עמדתי וקבלתי עם קנור המלאך; wording and name obscure], and the light went with me until I reached Gehinnom’s gates. The wicked who were there saw the light and rejoiced, telling one another: “This is the light that will bring us out of here.”’ But Zohar Chadash, Lekh Lekha, relates that he showed him forty-two chambers in the Garden of Eden for one who is meticulous in reciting the Shema’s first passage, which contains forty-two words. Afterwards he showed him seventy-two dwellings for one meticulous in the second passage down to ‘And you shall place,’ which contains seventy-two words. Afterwards he showed him fifty gates for one meticulous from ‘And you shall place’ down to ‘upon the earth,’ containing fifty words. Afterwards he showed him seventy-two palaces for one meticulous from ‘And He said’ down to ‘your God, true.’ Afterwards he likewise showed him the reverse in Gehinnom: chambers of darkness for those who are not meticulous. See Megalleh Amukkot, manner 223. See wonders in HaKotev, Ein Yaakov, the chapter Passin, in the name of an aggadah: ‘When I measured the first house in the abode of Gehinnom, a hundred mil in length and fifty mil in breadth.’ See there at great length for all seven houses and those judged within them. ‘And I saw houses,’ and so forth: in the seven houses of the Garden of Eden, in the first dwell converts, with Obadiah the prophet over them; in the second, penitents, with King Manasseh over them; in the third, the patriarchs, the wilderness generation, and all the kings of David’s house, with Moses and Aaron appointed over them; in the fourth, the completely righteous; in the fifth, Moses and Elijah; in the sixth, those who died sanctifying God’s name; in the seventh, those who died on account of Israel’s sins. ‘And three houses in Gehinnom’: the first dwelling is a hundred cubits long and fifty wide, and contains ten nations of idolaters and Absalom son of David; the second contains ten other nations of idolaters and Doeg; the third, ten nations and Korach with his congregation; the fourth, ten nations and Jeroboam; the fifth, ten nations and Ahab; the sixth, ten nations and Micah, and so forth.

This matter is startling: he wrote that he wanted the angel to write down Gehinnom for him but could not, because at that moment they killed Rabbi Yishmael the high priest and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and so forth. This was at the time of the Temple’s destruction, whereas Levi, Rabbi Yehoshua’s father, was Rabbi’s student, at any rate no less than a hundred years after the destruction; see above, part 1. Moreover, his words appear to mean that all ten martyrs of the government died at one time, and this is false; see Rabbi Akiva. Further, his statement that ‘at that moment they killed Rabbi Yishmael the high priest, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and ten righteous men’ is difficult, for we find only ten martyrs of the government. Shalshelet HaKabbalah 27a says that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi entered the Garden of Eden alive in Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s days; this is false.

But Rabbah, at the end of Shemot—Pekudei, section 52; at the end of Chayyei Sarah, section 62; Mikketz, section 92; and the Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Kol HaTzelamim—appears to show that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi died and did not enter the Garden of Eden alive: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, Zavdi ben Levi, and Rabbi Yose ben Petrom each recited a verse at their departure. Still, one can answer that it says only ‘at their departure.’ The Angel of Death told him three things: Berakhot 51a.

(4) In the Jerusalem Talmud, Terumot 8:10, and Bereshit Rabbah, Vayiggash, end of section 94, Elijah did not speak with him because he handed over Ulla ben Koshev, although this was the law, for he told him: ‘Is this the teaching of the pious?’ In the chapter HaGolin, 11a, because a man was eaten by a lion three parasangs from his place, and his merit had not protected him, Elijah did not speak with him for three days. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi fasted for many days and prayed to God to show him Elijah. Elijah then appeared before him and said: ‘If you desire something from me, I shall fulfill it for you.’ Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: ‘I long to travel with you and see your deeds in the world, and I shall learn wisdom from you.’ Elijah told him: ‘You will not be able to bear everything you see of my deeds, and I shall be troubled with explaining to you the reasons for my acts and actions.’ Rabbi Yehoshua replied: ‘I shall not ask, test, or trouble you with questions.’ Elijah made a condition with him: if he asked the reason for his deeds of signs and wonders, he would no longer travel with him. They both went until they reached the home of a poor, needy, destitute man, who had only one cow. The man and his wife sat at the entrance of the gate. They came out to meet them, greeted them, rejoiced with them, seated them in the best part of their home, and brought them food and drink. They lodged there. In the morning they arose to continue their journey, and Elijah prayed over the cow; it died immediately. They both left. Rabbi Yehoshua wondered at this, grew faint, and said to himself: ‘Was the poor man’s reward for honoring us only that his cow should be killed, when he has nothing else?’ He said to Elijah: ‘My lord, why did you kill the man’s cow, when he honored us?’ Elijah replied: ‘Remember the condition: listen and remain silent. But if you wish to part from me, I shall tell you.’ He ceased his questions and answered him no more. They traveled all day; in the evening they came to a rich man’s house. He paid them no attention and took no care to honor them; they sat without food or drink. The rich man had a fallen wall in his house which he needed to rebuild. In the morning Elijah prayed and built the wall, and they both left. Grief and wonder at Elijah’s deed grew in Rabbi Yehoshua’s heart, but he restrained his impulse to ask why he had done it. They traveled all day and in the evening reached a large synagogue. There were benches of silver and gold, and each person sat in his own chair. One said: ‘Who will feed these poor people tonight?’ Another replied: ‘Bread, water, and salt brought here will suffice for them.’ They did not honor them properly. They lodged there; in the morning they left, and Elijah told them: ‘May He make all of you heads.’ They continued on their way all day, and grief was added to Rabbi Yehoshua’s grief, but he did not answer. They came to a town as the sun was setting. The townspeople saw them and came out to meet them with kind hearts and great joy. They received them graciously, rejoiced with them, seated them in the best part of their home, in the house of the greatest among them; they ate, drank, and lodged there with great honor. In the morning Elijah prayed: ‘May God give you only one head.’ When Rabbi Yehoshua heard this, he could no longer restrain himself or remain silent about all the deeds and words. He said: ‘Tell me their secrets.’ Elijah replied: ‘If you intend to part from me, I shall explain everything and tell you the secret of these matters and the basis of the deeds you saw. Know that the man whose cow I killed—on that day his wife had been sentenced to die. I prayed to God that his cow should ransom his wife’s life. Moreover, I saw that through the woman much good and great benefit would come to his household. As for the rich man whose wall I built: had I left him to build it, he would have uncovered its foundation and found a great treasure of gold and silver. Therefore I built it for him; soon the wall will fall, and he will not build it again. The people for whom I prayed for many rulers and many heads: this is bad for them, bringing great disagreement in their counsels and thoughts, for any place with many heads is ruined and destroyed. As for the people for whom I prayed for one head: this is good for them and for their settlement, because their actions and counsels will come together in one counsel, and they will rejoice in it. No spirit of contention will enter among them; their counsel will not change, nor will their intention be frustrated. Hence those who speak in proverbs say: “With many helmsmen ships sink.” So too it says: “With one appointed leader a city is settled.”’ Elijah further instructed him: ‘I am going away from you; therefore I shall tell you what will benefit you. If you see a wicked man whose fortunes smile upon him, do not let your inclination entice you or wonder at him, for this is to his harm. If you see a righteous man distressed and suffering throughout his life, weary and laboring in hunger and thirst, nakedness and utter want, or afflicted by sufferings, do not become angry or vexed in spirit. Let neither your inclination nor your heart mislead you into thinking any doubt about your Maker. Consider in mind and heart that God is righteous, His judgment is just, and His eyes are upon a person’s ways. Who can tell Him, “What are You doing?”’ Afterwards they greeted one another, and he went on his way (Sefer Maasiyot of Rabbi Nissim ben Yaakov).

(5) In the Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit 3:4, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi held a fast in the south and rain fell. The people of Sepphoris said: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi brings down rain, while Rabbi Chanina withholds water from Sepphoris,’ and so forth. He sent and brought Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and told him: ‘Would my master be willing to go out with us to fast?’ They both went out for the fast, and no rain fell. He went in and told them: ‘Neither does Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi bring down rain, nor does Rabbi Chanina withhold rain from Sepphoris. Rather, the southerners’ hearts are soft: they hear words of Torah and submit. The people of Sepphoris have hard hearts: they hear words of Torah and do not submit.’ End quotation. The Babylonian Talmud, Taanit, has a similar matter concerning Rabbi Chama be-Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi; it appears to be one incident. Yuchasin, letter chet under Rabbi Chanina bar Chama, writes that Rabbi Chanina bar Chama brought rain to Sepphoris. Here, under Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, he writes that he lived in the south of the Land of Israel in Rabbi Chanina bar Chama’s time, and both fasted for rain in the south but were not answered, although Rabbi Chanina was answered in Sepphoris. They gave the reason that the southerners’ hearts were not submissive to Heaven, as is evident in the Jerusalem Talmud, Taanit, cited above. End quotation. See how he has turned the bowl upside down!

(6) In Rabbah, Vayishlach, section 78: ‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi went up to Rome. When he came to Akko, Rabbi Chanina went out to meet him. He found him limping upon his thigh and said: “You resemble your ancestor, ‘and he was limping upon his thigh.’”’ End quotation. Yedei Moshe writes: since his father Levi spoke defiantly toward Heaven and became lame—see his entry—one should not think that his son Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi also became lame because of a sin. Rather, ‘you resemble your ancestor Jacob,’ who became lame without sin. End quotation. Maharshal, Ketubbot 103b, writes that Levi sat with Rabbi Chanina, meaning he was his colleague. Rabbi Chanina was greater than he, for he would not submit to Rabbi Afes; see his entry. Rashi, Shabbat 59b, likewise writes that Levi and Rabbi Chanina were equal in wisdom and years. If so, how did Rabbi Chanina go out to meet Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who was much younger? Thus it appears that we should read ‘Levi went up to Rome,’ rather than his son Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi; this is correct. End quotation. At first sight his words seem right, for we have not found anywhere in the Talmud that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi became lame, only Levi, as above. But this is difficult: Rabbi Chanina was often before Rabbi—see his entry—and Levi too was Rabbi’s student. How had he not seen him limping until he came to Akko? He became lame through demonstrating a bow before Rabbi. Perhaps Rabbi Chanina was not before Rabbi at the time he became lame, and saw him when he came to Akko. As for his surprise that Rabbi Chanina went out to meet Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who was much younger: Rabbi Chanina told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, ‘My master’—meaning my lord—‘will you go out with us for the fast?’ He thus called Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ‘my lord.’ In the Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Ein Omdin, mishnah 1, Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came before an official of Caesarea, who rose before them. People asked him: ‘Do you rise before these Jews?’ He replied: ‘I saw faces of angels.’ End quotation. Thus their standing was equal; on the contrary, he called him ‘my master.’ There is therefore no reason to corrupt the books. In Yoma 49a, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asked about a high priest who took the handful and died, and so forth. Rabbi Chanina said: ‘See the question of the early ones.’ Does this imply that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was older? But Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: ‘Rabbi Chanina permitted it to me.’ We infer that Rabbi Chanina was older than Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. Rashi explains: it was not the way of elders to call young men ‘Rabbi’; rather, he should have said ‘Chanina permitted it to me.’ End quotation. See there for the answer: ‘Like the question of the early ones; I too am one of the early ones, and had difficulty with this.’ This requires examination: why must the Talmud prove that Rabbi Chanina was older than Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi from his calling him Rabbi Chanina? It is necessarily the case that he was much older. Ketubbot 103b relates that before Rabbi died he ordered Rabbi Chanina to preside. Rabbi Chanina did not accept, because Rabbi Afes was two and a half years older than he. In Rashi, Shabbat 59b, the words ‘and a half’ are missing. Rabbi Afes presided, and Rabbi Chanina sat outside—outside the study house, since he did not submit to Rabbi Afes. Levi came and sat with him. Rabbi Afes died and Rabbi Chanina presided; Levi had no one with whom to sit and came to Babylonia. They told Rav: ‘A great man has come.’ He said: ‘We may infer that Rabbi Afes has died, Rabbi Chanina is presiding, and Levi had no one with whom to sit, and so he came.’ But say instead that Rabbi Chanina died, while Rabbi Afes remained presiding as before; Levi then had no one with whom to sit and came. The answer is that Levi would have submitted to Rabbi Afes. Rashi, in the chapter Bammeh Ishah, explains: because he was older than he. Rashi writes there: because Rabbi Chanina was distinguished, he did not enter Rabbi Afes’s study house, but sat outside; out of respect for him, Levi sat with him. He came here—meaning he did not sit in the study house with Rabbi Chanina—because Rabbi Chanina was greater than he neither in Torah nor in years; Levi would not submit to him, and came here. End quotation. That is, had Rabbi Chanina been greater than he in years or Torah, Levi would have submitted to him. Had Levi been older than he, Rabbi Chanina would not have presided, just as Rabbi Chanina had declined to preside because Rabbi Afes was older. Thus we learn that Rabbi Chanina and Levi were equal in years. Accordingly, Rabbi Chanina was obviously older than Rabbi Yehoshua, Levi’s son. You have no greater proof than this. Understand this. Moreover, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s calling Rabbi Chanina ‘Rabbi’ is no proof that elders do not call young men ‘Rabbi’: Ulla was Rabbah’s teacher, and Rabbah was Rava’s teacher, as explained in each one’s place, yet we find that Ulla called Rava ‘Rabbi,’ in Chullin 131b, end. See the principles, where I wrote many proofs of this.

(7) He was from the Land of Israel: Tosafot, Sukkah 44a. He went up with Rabbi Yonatan to Jerusalem: Jerusalem Talmud, Maaser Sheni 3:6. He wrote in his notebook: ‘One who is born on the first day of the week,’ and so forth: Shabbat 156a. He was called Berabbi; see that entry. He went to a house of mourning only for one who departed without children: Moed Katan 27b. He said that he had learned sixty or eighty rulings from Rabbi Yehudah ben Pedayah and had forgotten them because he was occupied with communal needs; see Yehudah ben Neryah. He had his son read ‘One Torah shall there be for you,’ and so forth: Shabbat 68b, end. He taught his son: Horayot 8a. He rose before his son Rav Yosef because he had married into the Nasi’s family; see his entry. Shabbat 88b and 89a contain many expositions. He knew his own circumciser: Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Af Al Pi, halakhah 6.

(8) When Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan disagree, our established ruling follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: Tosafot, Eruvin 62b and 65b; Nedarim 45a, in Ran, Rosh, and Tosafot. Tosafot, Avodah Zarah 35a, end: the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi even against Rabbi Yochanan, all the more against Shmuel, since between Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. Seder Tannaim VeAmoraim likewise rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi everywhere; so too Tosafot, Gid HaNasheh, 97a. They further write that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi is a reliable authority and that the law follows him everywhere, even against Rabbi Yochanan. Responsa of the Geonim rules according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi everywhere. So too the Rosh, beginning of Lulav VaAravah: the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi against Rabbi Yochanan. Tosafot, Megillah 27a, Kiddushin 23a, and Gittin 39a, end: except for a few laws—‘the prayers were instituted in between,’ and, in the chapter Tzolin, ‘an iron barrier does not separate.’ Nevertheless, most Geonim ruled according to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi; so writes HaManhig. In the chapter Ellu Neemarin they brought this statement as a settled ruling regarding the priestly blessing. Concerning Kalenda, in Avodah Zarah, chapter 1, the law does not follow him, since a baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan. Likewise, his permitting a female convert younger than three to a priest is not the law. Likewise, his statement that one may not taste food at the time of the afternoon prayer until praying, in Shabbat, chapter 1, and Tefillat HaShachar. As for the law that nine and a minor may combine, only Rabbenu Tam and Rav Hai ruled like him. See Responsa Rashba, section 464: the Rosh’s statement that the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi against Rabbi Yochanan was not said by the Geonim. Taavah LaEinayim, Yoma 10b, writes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher; see the principles. Yuchasin likewise writes this in Maimonides’ name, Gittin, chapter 1. But Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, writes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was Rabbi Yochanan’s student; see below. So too Mordekhai, end of Yevamot, chapter 1. In Chelek 99b, ‘Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said’: it places Rabbi Yochanan before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

(9) Rabbi Abbahu came to their locale: Shabbat 46a, Yevamot 14a, and Jerusalem Talmud, Kirah, 46a. Rav Acha bar Chanilai; Rabbi Acha transmitted in his name. Rav Acha in Rabbi’s name: Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, chapter 1. Rav Acha Kartignaa; Rav Acha bar Chama was his student. Rabbi Ivon transmitted in his name. Rav Idi said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name; Rav Idi bar Avin transmitted in his name. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar appears to have been his teacher. Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat transmitted in his name. Rabbi Alexandri: see his entry. Rabbi Ammi transmitted in his name, as did Rabbi Assi. He transmitted in the name of Rabbi Antigonos. He was called Berabbi. Rabbi Bisna bar Chama; Rabbi Birim lived in his time. Rabbi Berekhiah was his grandson. Rabbi Gamliel Zuga; he appeared to Zavdi ben Levi in a dream—it appears that he was his brother. Rabbi Zevid said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Rabbi Zeira bar Chama transmitted in his name. He transmitted in Rabbi Chiyya’s name: Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Challon. He wished to see Rabbi Chiyya Rabbah after his death. He disputes with Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav. He leaned upon Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba’s shoulder: Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 1. Rabbi Chelba transmitted in his name. Rabbi Chama bar Ukva; Rabbi Chama bar Shakla; Rabbi Chanina; Rabbi Chana Kartignaa; Rav Chanan bar Zavdi lived in his time. Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name: Kohelet Rabbah, on ‘And I returned and saw.’ This requires examination, for Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai preceded him by much. But all this is absent in Yalkut. He transmitted in Rabbi Yehudah Nesia’s name, or the latter in his name. Rabbi Yehudah ben Levi: Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 1:1. Rabbi Yehudah ben Pazi transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yudan [גזורו; probably his circumciser, alternatively a byname]; Rabbi Yehudah ben Neryah was his teacher. Rabbi Yehudah be-Rabbi Simon; Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name: Sukkah 32a; see above, Rabbi Yochanan, his student or his teacher. In Rosh Hashanah 18b, Yoma 60b, and Menachot 95a they dispute. Rabbi Yonatan: see above. Rabbi Yonatan of Beit Guvrin; Rabbi Yose bar Chanina transmitted in his name: Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Yom HaKippurim, halakhah 1. That is also how it should read in Taanit 1:6. Rabbi Yose bar Simon transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yose ben Petros was his father-in-law. Rabbi Yose ben Nehorai questioned him. Rav Yosef was his son. ‘Rabbi Yosef said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name,’ 94a: it requires examination whether he was his student. He transmitted in Rabbi Yannai’s name. Rabbi Yaakov said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha bar Idi; Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yitzchak Chakula: Jerusalem Talmud, Peah 1:5. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani asked him. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachman transmitted in his name: Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Yom HaKippurim; see there. Rav Yitzchak transmitted in his name, as did Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ammi. Rabbi Yishmael bar Abba said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Rabbi Levi, his grandson, transmitted in his name. Rabbi Meyasha was his grandson. Rabbi Mellokh transmitted in his name, as did Rabbi Mana of Shaav. Rabbi Matton was his student. Rabbi Marion said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak transmitted in his name. His son Rabbi Simon transmitted in his name; Rabbi Simon transmitted in his name. Ulla said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Mar Ukva arranged aggadah before him. Rabbi Ukva transmitted in his name, as did Rabbi Azaryah. He transmitted in Rabbi Pedayah’s name, in Rabbi Pedat’s name, and in the name of the holy congregation. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name, in Bar Kappara’s name; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in Bar Kappara’s name. Rav; Rabbah bar bar Chana said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. ‘Rabbi said’: Yoma 69a and Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 1:1. ‘Rabbi said: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said three things in the name of the people of Jerusalem’: Pesachim 113a. This requires examination: his father Levi was Rabbi’s student, so how did Rabbi speak in his name? In Ein Yaakov the word Rabbi is absent, which pleased me. He said: ‘Rabbi sent Rabbi Romanos’: Yevamot 60b. Rami bar Abba transmitted in his name, as did Rabbi Shabbetai. Shimi bar Ukva; Rabbi Shalman bar Levi transmitted in his name. Rabbi Shmuel bar Natan; Shmuel said in his name. Shmuel bar Nachum was his student. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nadav asked him. Rabbi Simlai transmitted in his name: Bekhorot 36b. He transmitted in Resh Lakish’s name. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi: see above. Rabbi Shimon bar Abba brought a bill of divorce before him. Rabbi Shimon bar Acha transmitted in his name. He transmitted in Rabbi Shimon’s name: Bamidbar Rabbah, chapter 19. Rabbi Tanchum said in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiyya transmitted in his name.
